content: Surveillance for carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) can be conducted using broth-based culture techniques, which are widely accessible. Additionally, in-house molecular techniques and commercial chromogenic agar can be utilized. However, the latter two methods are not currently approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Screening tests in various studies have been performed on rectal or perirectal swabs. Limited data suggest that surveillance screening of stool specimens, rectal swabs, or perirectal swabs may yield higher detection rates compared to testing other body sites, such as nares or skin. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC) have issued updated guidelines for the prevention and control of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) infections. These recommendations aim to limit the emergence of these organisms and are based on strategies outlined in the 2006 HICPAC guidelines for managing multidrug-resistant organisms in healthcare settings. All patients colonized or infected with CRE or carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae should be placed under contact precautions. Acute care facilities should establish protocols, in line with Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines, to detect carbapenem resistance and carbapenemase production in Enterobacteriaceae, particularly Klebsiella species and Escherichia coli. Epidemiology and infection control staff should be promptly alerted when such cases are identified. Acute care facilities should review microbiology records from the previous 6–12 months to identify any previously unrecognized CRE cases. coli. The recommended surveillance culture methodology focuses on detecting carbapenem resistance or carbapenemase production in Klebsiella species and E. coli. This approach allows testing to be performed in microbiology laboratories without molecular methods and targets the organisms most commonly associated with CRE in the United States. When a hospital-associated CRE case is identified, facilities should conduct active surveillance testing of patients with epidemiologic links to the case, such as those in the same unit or cared for by the same healthcare personnel. The goal of active surveillance is to identify undetected carriers of carbapenem-resistant or carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella species and E. coli.g., weekly) until no new cases are identified. coli do not reemerge. Because CRE prevalence is low in most U.S. hospitals, routine microbiologic surveillance of admitted patients, such as that performed to detect methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) carriage, is not recommended. However, in regions like New York City, where CRE is more commonly recovered, including from community-admitted patients, point prevalence surveys in response to clinical cases may be less effective in controlling transmission. Facilities in regions where CRE is endemic should monitor clinical cases and implement intensified infection control strategies, as outlined in the 2006 HICPAC Tier 2 guidelines, if CRE rates are not decreasing. While allocating additional resources to prevent and control CRE poses challenges for hospitals, aggressive infection control strategies offer an opportunity to limit the impact of these pathogens while CRE prevalence remains low in most U.S. hospitals. Infection Prevention and Control All acute care facilities should implement contact precautions for patients colonized or infected with CRE or carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae. No specific recommendation can be made regarding when to discontinue contact precautions. Laboratory Clinical microbiology laboratories should follow CLSI guidelines for susceptibility testing and establish protocols for detecting carbapenemase production, such as performing the modified Hodge test. coli isolates that test positive for carbapenemase. Surveillance Acute care facilities should review clinical culture results from the preceding 6–12 months to identify previously unrecognized CRE cases. If previously unrecognized CRE cases are identified, a point prevalence survey should be conducted in high-risk units (e.g. If no previously unrecognized CRE cases are identified, facilities should continue monitoring for clinical infections. If CRE or carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella species or E. coli are detected from clinical cultures or point prevalence surveys reveal unrecognized colonization, facilities should investigate possible transmission by: Conducting active surveillance testing of patients with epidemiologic links to a CRE case (e.g., patients in the same unit or cared for by the same healthcare personnel). Continuing active surveillance periodically (e.g., weekly) until no new cases of colonization or infection suggesting cross-transmission are identified. If no transmission is identified after repeated active surveillance testing, consider altering the surveillance strategy by performing periodic point prevalence surveys in high-risk units. In areas where CRE is endemic, there is an increased likelihood of CRE importation, and the outlined procedures may not suffice to prevent transmission. Facilities in such areas should monitor clinical cases and consider additional strategies to reduce CRE rates, as described in the 2006 Tier 2 guidelines for managing multidrug-resistant organisms in healthcare settings.
